correctness.rationale: For fixed \(N\), the induced sum-incidence graph on two copies of \(\{0,\ldots,N\}\) has \(2N+2\) vertices and, being a forest, at most \(2N+1\) edges. Every \(d\in D\) with \(d\le N\) contributes exactly \(d+1\) distinct edges, proving the weighted inequality. Substituting \(N=d_n\) yields \(d_n\ge\sum_{j<n}(d_j+1)\), and induction gives \(d_n\ge2^n-1\); inversion gives the counting bound. Sharpness follows because \(2^{n+1}-1>2(2^n-1)\), so the cited Proposition 7.14 certifies forestness of the extremal support.
risks: The proof depends on the cited source's forest characterization and sufficient-gap proposition; both were checked in the full text. No computational or asymptotic step is used.

value.rationale: The source only extracts Sidon-scale sparsity and zero upper Banach density from the forest condition. The new theorem identifies the exact prefix occupancy envelope, upgrades the necessary sparsity from square-root scale to logarithmic scale, and supplies a single extremal support attaining the bound at every prefix scale. This gives a natural quantitative invariant of the newly characterized extremal dynamical class rather than an arbitrary finite slice.
risks: The proof is short; its value lies in the sharp structural consequence and extremal characterization, not in technical depth. It does not classify all forest supports or address higher alphabets.
